name: Slate navy
lede: Slate navy is a muted blue-grey drawn from Ridgway's 1912 standards and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, and in our color graph it is an exact duplicate, to the nearest measured unit, of a separately named color called Nigrosin Blue.

sections.title: Two names, one color
sections.body:
Our library carries this hue from Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* and from the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, filed as a grayish purplish blue, though neither source's plate or block number survives in our records [1]. The "navy" in the name marks it as a place-or-institution word, and nothing in our sources explains the choice further [2].

In our color graph, Slate navy measures a CIEDE2000 distance of exactly zero from a different catalogued name, Nigrosin Blue: the same color, reached twice under two names [3]. Its next-closest relatives are [[diamin-azo-blue]], a touch purpler, and [[glacier]], almost the same [3].

A little further out are [[acetin-blue]], lighter at 5.1 units, and [[bruges]], bluer at 5.3 [3]. Our library records no first-recorded date for this entry either, unlike the plate-dated names elsewhere, a gap we note rather than paper over [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Slate navy covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 225 works, peaking in the 1920s at nearly six times the archive's overall rate [4]. It is disproportionately a Scandinavian color on these numbers: Henri-Edmond Cross, Karl Isakson and Vilhelm Lundstrøm all carry it at more than fifteen times their expected rate, and it covers 60 per cent of Balthasar Denner's 1700 *Portrait of Peder Tordenskjold* [4]. It most often shares a canvas with denim blue and charcoal grey [4]. As always, these are screen colors read from photographs of varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [4]. Across its matches, slightly more than half the coverage falls in shadow and most of the rest in mid-tones, with almost none as a highlight [4].
